10 Most Financially Stable SACCOS to Trust with Your Savings, New Report
items.description: SASRA’s 2025 report ranks Kenya’s deposit-taking Saccos for financial stability, showing how Winas and Newfortis rival sector giants on key financial metrics.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

The Sacco Societies Regulatory Authority (SASRA) has published its SACCO Supervision Annual Report 2025 , released on October 6, ranking Kenya's Deposit-Taking Saccos (DT-Saccos) across a range of financial health indicators.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The report measures five core metrics: Core Capital to Total Assets (CCA), Core Capital to Total Deposits (CCD), Institutional Capital to Total Assets (ICA), external borrowing levels, and Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratios. Based on these indicators, the following ten institutions stand out as the most financially stable.
Winas DT-Sacco leads the rankings, posting a CCD ratio of 84.94% against the regulatory minimum of 8%, alongside a CCA of 42.22%, zero external borrowing, and an NPL ratio of just 1.61%.
Tenwek Hospital announces morgue attendant role and several vacancies, how to apply
Kenya National Police (KNP) DT-Sacco, the third-largest by total assets, follows closely with a CCA of 35.67%, an ICA of 30.11%, no external debt, and an NPL of 2.33%.
Transnation DT-Sacco ranks third, meeting all capital thresholds comfortably with a CCA of 21.10% and an NPL of 2.90%, while Hazina DT-Sacco records a CCA of 16.15% and an NPL ratio of just 2.00%.
Sheria DT-Sacco, which serves Kenya's legal fraternity, maintains a CCA of 18.17% and zero external borrowing, with NPLs at 2.80%.
Newfortis DT-Sacco distinguishes itself with the lowest NPL ratio on the entire list at 0.48%, supported by a CCA of 13.48% and no external debt.
Imarisha DT-Sacco records a CCA of 17.49% and an NPL of 1.53%, with minimal external borrowing of 2.44%.

Mwalimu National DT-Sacco, the largest Sacco in Kenya by total assets, improved its NPL ratio to 2.42% in 2025, reinforcing confidence in the teachers' institution. Its CCA stands at 13.96% and ICA at 9.89%.
Stima DT-Sacco, the second-largest, holds a CCA of 19.22% and an ICA of 12.84%.
KCB’s KSh 58.6b profit: What it means for your loan, hustle, job prospects
Its NPL ratio of 6.48% is higher than others on the list, though the institution carries negligible external borrowing at 1.39%.
Unison DT-Sacco rounds out the top ten with a CCA of 16.15%, zero external debt, and an NPL of 2.16%.
A consistent pattern across the top performers is the near-total absence of external borrowing, with most institutions relying entirely on member deposits.
The report also highlights that NPL ratios below 3% serve as a reliable indicator of responsible lending practices.

SASRA's data further underscores that financial stability does not correlate directly with size, as smaller institutions such as Winas and Newfortis outperform some of the sector's largest players on key capital and asset-quality metrics.
SASRA warned that SACCO members should look beyond high dividends and consider their institution’s financial health .
The regulator cautioned that excessive payouts could weaken a SACCO’s ability to lend, withstand unexpected losses and protect members’ savings.

items.title: Governor Kihika commissions water, agricultural projects in Kuresoi North
items.description: Governor Kihika commissions water, agricultural projects in Kuresoi North Kenya News Agency
content: The Nakuru County government is implementing various development projects in water, agriculture, healthcare, education and road infrastructure across Kuresoi North Sub-County.
The initiatives are aimed at improving residents’ livelihoods, boosting agricultural production and expanding access to essential public services.

During a development tour of the sub-county, Governor Susan Kihika commissioned the Nyakinywa Water Project at Nyakinywa Centre and the Sirikwa Agricultural Aggregation Centre, while inspecting other ongoing development projects aimed at improving service delivery to residents.

Speaking during the commissioning of the projects, Kihika said her administration was prioritizing investments that directly address the needs of residents, particularly access to clean water, better agricultural markets, improved healthcare and education facilities.

She said the Nyakinywa Water Project, whose first phase involved drilling and solarising a borehole, installing pipelines and constructing a storage tank, was expected to serve more than 5,000 residents and local institutions.
“Access to reliable water is essential not only for domestic use, but also for supporting agricultural production and improving the livelihoods of our people,” she said.

The Governor highlighted that the county had also invested in agricultural infrastructure through the Sirikwa Agricultural Aggregation Centre, which seeks to improve produce handling, eliminate exploitative brokers and increase farmers’ earnings.
She noted that the facility had helped raise potato prices from Sh1,200 to Sh7,000 per bag by improving aggregation and market access.
Kihika explained that her administration is constructing agricultural aggregation centres across the county to leverage value addition and increase farmers’ incomes.
She observed that the Sirikwa facility demonstrates how organised marketing and improved produce handling can transform farmers’ earnings.

“I have directed that part of the facility be utilised for the last-mile distribution of subsidised fertiliser to ensure farmers access essential farm inputs more conveniently. Our intention is to replicate this model across all 55 wards,” she said.

Kihika further highlighted investments in road infrastructure, saying the county had allocated resources towards grading and gravelling access roads and constructing Shalom Bridge to improve connectivity and facilitate the movement of agricultural produce to markets.
On healthcare, she said construction of a modern maternity wing at Sirikwa Health Centre will improve maternal healthcare services and provide mothers with a dignified environment for childbirth.
She added that Choronok and Gacharage dispensaries were undergoing renovations, while Kuresoi North Level Four Hospital was nearing completion.

In education, the Governor said the county had completed the Aerial, Karima and Kiletien Early Childhood Development Education (ECDE) centres and would introduce free uniforms for all ECDE learners starting January.
She said the county had also enrolled 1,061 learners in the Uji feeding programme and allocated Sh1.5 million in bursaries to support needy students.

The Governor also highlighted the distribution of avocado seedlings, sunflower seeds and maize seeds to farmers to promote crop diversification, improve food security and create additional income opportunities.
She said the county was also working to improve security and commercial activities through the installation of high-mast floodlights and streetlights in key trading centres.

Kihika further noted that the Gacharage Economic Stimulus Programme (ESP) Market was at the planning stage, while the county continued to prioritise the development of markets to provide traders with better working environments.
In Nyota Ward, she reported that six water projects had been completed, including the Chesirikwa Water Project, with four others ongoing.
The county had also completed seven road upgrades and constructed a footbridge at Kabaris-Chesirikwa.
Other achievements included the completion of 11 ECDE centres, construction of four sanitation blocks and the installation of 10 floodlights and streetlights across major commercial centres.
The Governor added that the county was fast-tracking title deeds for 306 residents in Sitoito and Langwenda while securing land for public utilities.
She also urged residents to support President William Ruto’s development agenda, citing the 26 ongoing Economic Stimulus Programme (ESP) markets across Nakuru County.

Kihika reaffirmed that the projects form part her administration’s wider development agenda aimed at strengthening agricultural productivity, improving access to essential services and expanding economic opportunities across Kuresoi North Sub-County.

items.title: Gladys Wanga Most Influential Woman Leader, Ann Waiguru Second; Mwelekeo Insights Poll
items.description: Gladys Wanga beats Ann Waiguru in Mwelekeo Insights' November 2026 poll on Kenya's most influential woman leaders, attracting 40.3% of responses.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Homa Bay Governor Gladys Wanga has edged out Kirinyaga Governor Ann Waiguru in a closely contested national poll ranking Kenya's most influential woman leaders.
The November 2026 survey by Mwelekeo Insights placed Wanga first with 40.3% of the responses, equivalent to 27,066 votes, narrowly ahead of Waiguru, who garnered 39.4%, representing 26,482 votes.
The difference was just 584 responses, or 0.9 percentage points, highlighting the close contest between the two governors.
Former Health Cabinet Secretary Susan Nakhumicha came a distant third with 2.0%, attracting 1,319 responses, while Samburu West MP Naisula Lesuuda finished fourth with 1.7% (1,157 responses).

Machakos Governor Wavinya Ndeti followed closely in fifth position with 1,154 responses, also representing 1.7%.
Fred Matiang'i gains ground as Edwin Sifuna leads new 2027 presidential poll
Businesswoman Agnes Kagure ranked sixth nationally, receiving 1,066 responses (1.6%), followed by Suba North MP Millie Odhiambo with 1,027 (1.5%).
Former Kitui Governor Charity Ngilu secured 916 responses (1.4%), while nominated Senator Catherine Omanyo received 903 (1.3%).

Other notable figures included Law Society of Kenya President Faith Odhiambo with 828 responses, former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza with 809 and former presidential candidate Martha Karua with 808. All three recorded 1.2%.

Nakuru Governor Susan Kihika and businesswoman Wangui Ngirici each received less than 1%, while Chief Justice Martha Koome attracted 332 responses (0.5%). Esther Passaris, Esther Muchemi and Beatrice Elachi completed the list.
Further down the rankings, Fatuma Achani received 753 responses (1.1%), followed by Susan Kihika with 599 and Wangui Ngirici with 585, both recording 0.9%.
Cecily Mbarire garnered 540 responses (0.8%), Tabitha Karanja 502 (0.7%), while Chief Justice Martha Koome received 332 (0.5%).
Esther Passaris recorded 192 responses (0.3%), Esther Muchemi 104 (0.2%) and former Nairobi Speaker Beatrice Elachi finished last with 78 responses (0.1%).

According to Mwelekeo Insights, the poll ran from November 18 to November 21, 2026, attracting 67,220 responses from participants across the country.
It featured 21 women drawn from different areas of leadership, including governors, legislators, judicial officials, business leaders and former government officials.

However, the organisation clarified that the exercise was an open online poll in which participants voluntarily submitted their preferences. It was not a statistically representative survey of the Kenyan population, and no conventional margin of error applies.

items.title: Johnson Sakaja Reviews 2022 Manifesto as He Eyes 2nd Term, Identifies Hardest Promise to Fulfil
items.description: Nairobi governor Johnson Sakaja identified Dishi na County as his hardest 2022 campaign promise as he eyes a second term and plans to expand the programme.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has reflected on his administration's campaign pledges, identifying the school feeding programme as his most challenging promise to implement.
Speaking while reviewing his 2022 manifesto, Sakaja admitted that implementing Dishi na County, his flagship school feeding programme, was among the most difficult undertakings of his administration.
William Ruto announces oncoming recruitment for all BOM teachers
The governor said the initiative demanded substantial financial and political capital, with legal challenges and negotiations threatening to delay its implementation.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Launched on August 28, 2023, Dishi na County provides subsidised, freshly prepared meals to learners in public primary schools and early childhood development centres.

Parents contribute KSh5 per meal, with the county government and development partners supporting the remaining costs. The initiative operates through a network of central kitchens, which prepare and distribute meals to participating schools.
By August 2026, the programme had served more than 85 million meals. It currently feeds over 324,000 learners daily across 230 public schools in all 17 sub-counties.
Sakaja said the initiative had become an example of how government interventions could improve children's welfare while demonstrating that campaign commitments could be fulfilled.
Kenyan newspapers, November 21: Kalonzo's trip to US postponed as Sifuna is awaited
Looking ahead, the governor said his administration was preparing to extend the feeding programme to public day secondary schools, with January 2027 set as the target.
The review of his manifesto comes as Sakaja positions himself for another term at City Hall.

In November 2026, the governor joined the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), ditching the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) party. He defended the move, describing it as a political transition that would not affect his relationship with the broad-based government.
Sakaja also launched the Let's Talk podcast, which provides a platform for engaging Nairobi residents on development, service delivery and his administration's record.

However, the 2027 Nairobi gubernatorial contest is already attracting interest from several politicians, including Embakasi East MP Babu Owino , Embakasi North MP James Gakuya and Kasarani MP Ronald Karauri.

items.title: "2 TAM": Linda Mwananchi office covered with graffiti ahead of Ruto's visit
items.description: A Linda Mwananchi Movement office in Matungu sub county, Kakamega County, was defaced with ‘2 TAM’ graffiti marks ahead of President William Ruto's visit.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
A Linda Mwananchi Movement office in Kakamega County has been defaced by unknown individuals, with fresh political graffiti appearing on its walls ahead of President William Ruto’s visit to the area.
The building, located in Matungu Sub-county, had been painted in the movement’s distinctive white and blue colours, with its name and logo prominently displayed.
However, unknown individuals reportedly struck during the night, using black paint to cover the Linda Mwananchi branding and replace it with the bold inscription ‘2 TAM’.
The incident comes as Ruto prepares to visit the area as part of his ongoing development tour of Western Kenya , during which he is expected to launch a road project.

Images of the building showed black paint covering sections of the original branding, including the movement's name and logo.
The words ‘2 TAM’ were prominently written across the affected sections of the building.

The inscription appears to reference calls for Ruto to serve a second presidential term, although those responsible for the graffiti and their intentions had not been established by the time of publication.
It was also unclear whether the incident had been reported to the police or whether any suspects had been identified.
The incident comes as the president undertakes a development tour of the Western region, with several infrastructure projects and government initiatives forming part of his engagements.
During his expected visit to Matungu, Ruto is scheduled to launch a road project, although further details about the project were not immediately available.

items.description: Baba Talisha undergoes urgent cornea transplant in Kenya to save his left eye after a severe infection caused perforation, as he seeks funds for care abroad.

Kenyan influencer Baba Talisha shared a deeply personal update on Saturday, November 21, 2026, revealing he was undergoing a cornea transplant at a hospital in Kenya in a bid to save his remaining good eye.

In the post shared on Instagram , Baba Talisha disclosed that an aggressive infection, one that doctors have struggled to identify and bring under control, had caused his cornea to perforate, forcing his medical team to recommend the surgery as an urgent intervention.

He had previously revealed that he lost the ability to see in his right eye, a development that sent shockwaves through his online following.
Now, with pressure in his right eye remaining dangerously high despite medical efforts to lower it, and with his left cornea perforated, the situation has taken a more critical turn.

His doctors advised that the transplant was necessary not only to protect his left eye but also to stabilise his condition ahead of a planned trip to India, where he is expected to undergo further investigations and access more specialised care.

Despite the weight of the situation, the influencer struck a hopeful tone in his message, saying he was taking the journey "one day at a time, with hope and gratitude for everyone walking beside us."

The post, which was shared while wearing what appeared to be an LCIF Lions Clubs International Foundation SightFirst-branded item, also hinted at more details to come, with the caption cutting off mid-sentence, leaving followers eager for his next update.

Baba Talisha's wife, Miss Wanjey, recently revealed during a TikTok livestream that a parasitic amoeba linked to contaminated water and dust embedded in Baba Talisha's cornea caused total vision loss in his eye.
She noted that they were awaiting lab results sent to India before starting new treatment, planning a second opinion at Kikuyu Hospital, and considering a corneal transplant if medication fails.
While hoping he regains most of his sight, Miss Wanjey stepped in to manage his business communications as he deals with light sensitivity and recovery.

items.title: STEM key to realisation of Kenya’s first-world status, PS Oluga
items.description: STEM key to realisation of Kenya’s first-world status, PS Oluga Kenya News Agency
content: The government is investing heavily in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) to realise its Singapore dream.

Medical Services Principal Secretary (PS), Dr. Ouma Oluga, speaking during a fundraiser for a STEM Training Center at Okela Comprehensive School in Rarieda Sub-county, said STEM is the backbone of the country’s future global standing.

“Today in the first world there are discussions on permanent underclass, which simply means if you are left behind in technology, then you will forever never catch up with the rest of the world, a situation which we want to avoid with our students, the youth and even our teachers,” enlightens Dr. Oluga.
The government must, therefore, endeavour to ensure students earmarked to build the country towards the first-world status are well trained on the emerging technologies.
“That’s why under the clarion call ‘Usawa ni Sawa’, the government is creating opportunities everywhere for students who want to realise their full potential.

Right now Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being used in manufacturing, assembling, agriculture and even in governance, which then means we can no longer ignore technology, which is the backbone for our future,” he stressed.
The PS observed that there is a need to properly equip schools across the Nyanza region and to upgrade infrastructure to train learners to help them realise their full potential in STEM education.

“Across the counties of Migori, Homa Bay, Kisumu and Siaya, there is a need to have adequate schools with proper STEM training facilities, which can effectively direct learners towards STEM education,” he emphasised.

Dr Oluga disclosed that the anticipated Sh250 million STEM training facility at Okela Comprehensive School will not only benefit learners from the locality but will also open doors to other students from the region.

“In this particular school, at the moment, we only have three students who are undertaking physics, and in the last 14 years, no single student has scored an ‘A’ minus or even a ‘B’ plain in sciences, yet the world is now being run through innovation and critical thinking.

We hope that this facility will change the negative trend. I have also spoken to over 700 head teachers from Siaya County to utilise the facility for their students’ exposure once it’s completed,” said the PS.
Dr Oluga further revealed that the facility will also be used to train teachers from the region on AI skills to enable them to deliver their services effectively.

Siaya digital hub to spur innovation, entrepreneurship and economic growth
items.description: Siaya digital hub to spur innovation, entrepreneurship and economic growth Kenya News Agency
content: The Siaya Artificial Intelligence Youth Agency (SAIYA), was today launched in a colourful event held at SAIYA House in Siaya County and witnessed by the Medical Services Principal Secretary (PS), Dr Ouma Oluga, and his National Treasury counterpart, Dr Chris Kiptoo.

The initiative is aimed at empowering young people through Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital skills, opening new avenues for innovation, entrepreneurship, employment and economic transformation within the county and beyond.

Speaking during the occasion, Dr Oluga underscored the significance of the Hub in shaping the future of Siaya’s youth, noting that it will serve as a platform for equipping young people with skills that can enable them to become agents of transformation in their communities.

The PS, who also serves as the Patron of the Agency, urged the youth to embrace emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence, noting that technological advancement, will play a critical role in shaping opportunities and livelihoods in the years ahead.
“As we talk about Youth Agency, it means the power for you to deliver the future you want to live in,” Dr Oluga said.

He further reaffirmed his commitment to creating opportunities and platforms through which young people can turn their ideas into practical solutions, contributing to both personal growth and national development.
“As your patron, my work is to create the platform for you to bring your ideas into life,” Oluga said.

While acknowledging that the journey towards innovation and success may not be easy, Dr Oluga expressed confidence in the resilience of the youth, urging them to remain determined in the face of challenges, as they pursue their aspirations.

“I have zero promise that I know how long that journey will take you. I have zero promise that you won’t get tired along the way, that you will not face any challenges that will hinder you from achieving what you need,” he said.

Also present during the launch was, Nelly Maluka Oluoch, Acting Chief Executive Officer of the Kenya Film Classification Board (KFCB), who challenged the youth to view the Hub as more than just an AI facility, describing it as a broader platform for empowerment and opportunity.
“This Centre goes beyond AI because that is just an enabler, which has opportunities and risks, but a real form of Empowerment,” Maluka said.

She cautioned the youth about the potential risks associated with Artificial Intelligence, urging them to uphold professionalism, responsibility and ethical standards, as they engage with the technology.

Maluka further encouraged young people to utilise the skills and opportunities offered by the hub to drive economic growth, innovation and self-reliance, while actively contributing to the country’s development.
“This can be our Singapore. Don’t wait for any other Singapore. Use the skills that you will gain from this Hub to help you grow yourselves and the entire nation,” she emphasised.

The establishment of SAIYA is expected to provide a platform through which young people can develop solutions, to long-standing community challenges, leveraging digital technology and innovation, to address local needs.

The initiative seeks to harness the potential of Artificial Intelligence, equip young people with digital competencies and unlock opportunities in innovation, entrepreneurship and economic transformation across Siaya County.

Testing a trading app on your phone? Six tech checks Kenyan users should make first
items.description: Trading apps can open up markets that were once out of reach for ordinary Kenyans, from Nairobi Securities Exchange shares to global stocks
content: Kenya’s fintech scene moves fast. M-Pesa changed how the country pays for things, digital lenders changed how it borrows, and now trading apps are changing how a growing number of Kenyans invest. Downloads have climbed as young users look for ways to grow their money beyond SACCOs and savings accounts.

Most coverage of these apps focuses on returns and strategies. This piece looks at something more basic: the technology itself. A trading app holds your identity documents, your money and often access to your M-Pesa line. That makes its security and performance just as important as its features.

Only install trading apps from the Google Play Store or the Apple App Store. Fraudsters regularly circulate APK files through WhatsApp and Telegram that look exactly like legitimate apps but are built to steal login details and one-time passwords. On the store page, check the developer name, the number of downloads, the date of the last update and whether reviews mention withdrawal problems.

Then check the company behind it. In Kenya, the Capital Markets Authority licenses stockbrokers and online forex brokers and publishes the list on its website. Matching the app’s developer to a licensed firm takes two minutes and filters out most scams.

A trading app needs your camera for KYC, internet access and notifications. It has no good reason to read your SMS inbox, your contacts or your call logs. Some fake investment apps request these permissions to intercept M-Pesa messages or harass contacts. On Android, review permissions under Settings, then Apps, and switch off anything that does not make sense.

At minimum, the app should support two-factor authentication through an authenticator app or SMS, and biometric login with fingerprint or face unlock. Authenticator apps are safer than SMS codes, which can be exposed through SIM swap fraud, a problem Kenyan banks and telcos have warned about for years. If an app only offers a simple password, keep looking.

Many trading apps are designed in Europe or Asia and tested on fast connections. In Kenya, users switch between Safaricom, Airtel and home Wi-Fi, and data bundles matter. Test the app on mobile data before funding it. Watch how quickly prices update, whether charts lag, and how the app behaves when the connection drops in the middle of an order. A good app tells you clearly whether an order went through. A poor one leaves you guessing.
Data use is worth checking too. Live charts and streaming prices can consume a surprising amount of a daily bundle, so look for settings that reduce chart refresh rates or switch to a lighter mode.

M-Pesa deposits are now standard among apps that target Kenya, but integration quality varies. The best apps use official Safaricom payment channels with a recognisable paybill or till number and send clear confirmation messages. Be wary of apps that ask you to send money to a personal number or an agent. Test withdrawals with a small amount before depositing more. How quickly and smoothly money comes back tells you a lot about the platform.

Once the basics are covered, compare features. Useful ones include demo accounts with virtual funds, price alerts, clear charting tools, stop-loss orders, transparent fee breakdowns and in-app support that responds within hours, not days. A wider comparison of trading apps in Kenya , with features set out side by side, can help narrow the list. Use it alongside the CMA register rather than in place of it.

Trading apps can open up markets that were once out of reach for ordinary Kenyans, from Nairobi Securities Exchange shares to global stocks. But the same convenience that makes them attractive makes them a target for fraud. Treat a new trading app the way you would treat a new banking app: verify who built it, lock it down, and test it with small amounts before trusting it with your savings.

items.title: ADVANCING CRITICAL CARE EXPERTISE FOR MILITARY HEALTHCARE EXCELLENCE
items.description: ADVANCING CRITICAL CARE EXPERTISE FOR MILITARY HEALTHCARE EXCELLENCE Ministry of Defence – Kenya
content: Specialised medical expertise is vital to saving lives, improving patient outcomes and sustaining operational readiness within the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF). As military healthcare demands continue to evolve, investment in advanced clinical training remains essential to developing a skilled, responsive and professionally competent healthcare workforce.

The Defence College of Health Sciences (DCHS), a College of the National Defence University-Kenya (NDU-K), officially opened the November 2026 cohort of the Higher Diploma in Kenya Registered Critical Care Nursing (HDCCN) programme, marking another milestone in advancing specialised nursing education within the Defence Forces.

The programme is designed to equip nursing personnel with advanced clinical knowledge, specialised competencies and practical skills essential for managing critically ill patients and delivering high-quality care in demanding healthcare environments.

Through the training, participants will enhance their professional proficiency in critical care nursing, contributing to improved patient management, clinical decision-making and the delivery of specialised medical services across military healthcare facilities.

Beyond individual professional development, the programme represents a strategic investment in institutional healthcare capacity, ensuring that the KDF maintains a pool of highly trained medical personnel capable of responding to complex healthcare needs in both operational and non-operational settings.
The initiative reflects DCHS’s central role in advancing medical education, professional excellence and specialised healthcare training within the Defence Forces.

By investing in critical care expertise, the KDF continues to build a resilient, competent and future-ready military healthcare system capable of safeguarding the health of its personnel and delivering quality medical services to those under its care.

Beyond the Prescription: Why Diabetes Care in Kenya Must Start with the Patient
items.description: By Omboki Monayo Nairobi- Diabetes is emerging as a significant public-health challenge in Kenya, affecting hundreds of thousands of people and
content: Nairobi – Diabetes is emerging as a significant public-health challenge in Kenya, affecting hundreds of thousands of people and putting growing pressure on the healthcare system. Beyond blood sugar control, the condition raises concerns about heart health, nutrition, reproductive health, dementia, and patients’ overall quality of life.

According to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) Diabetes Atlas , 11th Edition (2025), about 813,300 Kenyan adults aged 20–79 are living with diabetes, a prevalence of 3.1 per cent. An estimated 440,000 adults may not know they have the condition, which underscores the need for more screening and early diagnosis.

The risk rises with age and other metabolic factors. The condition takes several forms, including Type 1, Type 2, and gestational diabetes. The 2025 Type 1 Diabetes Index estimates that 22,063 people of all ages in Kenya live with Type 1 diabetes, while Type 2 accounts for the majority of cases.

For Dr Prisca Mungla, a consultant physician, diabetes specialist and endocrinologist, addressing this burden takes more than prescriptions. Patients need personalised treatment, practical lifestyle advice and consistent physician follow-up.
“Diabetes management is not just about prescribing medication. We need to understand the patient, their lifestyle, their preferences and the challenges they face,” she says.
Dr Mungla was speaking at a World Diabetes Day Symposium Series webinar organised by Kenyatta National Hospital and the University of Nairobi.
Dr Mungla advocates starting physical activity early. Exercise, she says, is essential for maintaining muscle strength, improving cardiovascular health and supporting blood sugar control.
“Start exercising early to build muscle strength. We should not wait until people are older or begin experiencing complications before encouraging them to exercise.”
She particularly encourages older people to take up resistance training, even through simple seated exercises.
“Encourage the elderly to do weight-training exercises. They can even do some while sitting. The important thing is to keep their muscles active and maintain their strength.”
Strength matters because falls can cause serious injuries, and these are more likely when low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) brings on dizziness and confusion.
Dr Mungla recommends 30–45 minutes of physical activity five days a week, combining aerobic exercise such as walking or swimming with strength training.
“Even if you can only manage 10–15 minutes of exercise regularly, it is still a win. The more consistently you exercise, the better the benefits.”
Patients taking medication that can lower blood sugar should monitor their glucose levels and carry a suitable snack when exercising.
While medication is central to diabetes management, Dr Mungla cautions against giving everyone the same treatment.

“Some patients are already struggling with their weight, so we need to be careful about prescribing medication that could cause further weight loss. Where appropriate, we should consider weight-neutral medicines.”
She also urges healthcare professionals to take patients’ complaints about side effects seriously.

“If patients say they are experiencing side effects, please believe them. We have a whole array of medicines. If one medication is not working for a patient, we should consider changing it until we find one they can tolerate.”
Metformin, commonly prescribed for Type 2 diabetes, can cause nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal problems.

“I prefer starting with 500mg and increasing the dose gradually, depending on how the patient responds,” she explains. Taking metformin with meals, or using an extended-release formulation, may also improve tolerability for some patients, she adds.

Ozempic’s popularity has drawn interest from people seeking weight loss, including those without diabetes. Dr Mungla says treatment must be guided by the patient’s diagnosis, clinical markers and individual needs.

“Diabetes is not one condition. We have Type 1, Type 2 and gestational diabetes, among other forms. We classify and manage these conditions based on the patient’s clinical presentation and relevant markers.”

Ozempic contains semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite. Oral semaglutide is sold as Rybelsus, and the wider treatment family includes dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists. The injectable is taken once a week, while the oral form has specific daily administration requirements. Both can cause gastrointestinal side effects.
“Some patients are comfortable with injections, while others prefer tablets. We need to talk to patients about what they prefer rather than forcing treatment options down their throats,” she says.

“Treatment decisions should consider safety, affordability, clinical suitability and patient preference,” she adds. Semaglutide may also be prescribed for weight management in eligible people without diabetes, using an approved formulation under medical supervision.

Food and alcohol can be difficult subjects for people with diabetes, especially with more social gatherings expected during the festive season. Dr Mungla believes patients need practical advice, not blanket bans.

“Alcohol is one of the interesting conversations we have with patients. We need to understand their circumstances, how well controlled their diabetes is and whether they are taking medication that could cause hypoglycaemia.”

She cautions against binge drinking and says the subject needs careful handling, particularly for patients whose blood sugar is poorly controlled. For patients who struggle with alcohol use, her advice is firm: “In such a case, I will recommend cutting it out completely.”

Beer contains carbohydrates from malted grains, and cocktails often contain added sugar. Alcohol can also cause delayed hypoglycaemia, particularly in people taking insulin or certain other diabetes medications.
On fruit, she urges moderation rather than elimination.

“Most of the fruits available here are the tropical variety and naturally quite sweet. But does that mean we should tell patients not to eat fruit? No. We need to be practical and consider what is available, what is affordable, and what the patient can manage.”
She recommends controlling portions and eating one fruit at a time rather than large servings of mixed fruit salad. Thorn melon, strawberries, and blueberries are options where accessible.

Diabetes care also means protecting the brain and the cardiovascular system. People with diabetes face a higher risk of cardiovascular complications, including stroke, which can contribute to cognitive impairment.

“People living with diabetes can have an increased risk of cardiovascular complications. These vascular problems can also affect the brain. Small strokes, for instance, can contribute to cognitive impairment,” Dr Mungla explains.

She is particularly concerned about dementia care in Kenya, where families often carry the burden of round-the-clock caregiving. As the condition progresses, patients become increasingly dependent on others for everyday activities, placing heavy emotional and physical demands on caregivers.
“In our African culture, when you take an elderly person to a retirement home or specialised care facility, people may assume that you have abandoned them. But that is not necessarily the case.

“Sometimes these patients need specialised care that the family may not be able to provide at home. Taking them somewhere they can receive proper attention should not be interpreted as abandoning them.”
She believes Kenya needs greater awareness, stronger dementia services and better support for families and caregivers.
Dr Mungla also stresses careful management for women planning pregnancy, particularly those with pre-existing diabetes or a history of gestational diabetes.
“Gestational diabetes is something we should not ignore after delivery. A woman who develops diabetes during pregnancy has an increased risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.”
Children exposed to gestational diabetes in the womb may also face higher metabolic risks later, so follow-up matters for both mother and child.

For women with pre-existing diabetes who are considering pregnancy or in-vitro fertilisation (IVF), she recommends thorough preparation, including assessment of blood sugar, insulin requirements, blood pressure and cholesterol.
“We need to review the medication she is taking and make sure everything is appropriate before she conceives.”

The HbA1c test, which measures average blood sugar over the previous three months, is especially important for IVF, because poorly controlled glucose can reduce egg quality and embryo implantation and raise the risk of miscarriage.

“Where safely achievable, an HbA1c below 6.5 per cent is a common preconception target for fertility specialists. This will provide the best chance of a successful cycle and healthy pregnancy,” she says. “Appropriate folic acid supplementation and medication reviews are also essential.”
IVF can add hormonal changes that complicate glucose management, which makes coordinated specialist care vital.
“We need teamwork. The gynaecologist, endocrinologist and nutritionist must work together to monitor the patient and follow her throughout the process.”
Continuous glucose monitoring and insulin pumps may also help eligible patients where available and affordable.
Ultimately, Dr Mungla believes successful diabetes management must be built around the individual, not the disease alone.
“Diabetes management is not simply about telling people what they cannot eat or giving them medication. We need to understand their lives and help them make choices they can sustain.”
For Kenya, that means better access to screening, affordable treatment, nutritional guidance and specialised care, along with tackling the cultural barriers around chronic illness.

“A patient who cannot afford imported fruits needs realistic dietary advice. An elderly person who struggles to walk needs an exercise programme suited to their abilities. Someone experiencing medication side effects needs a doctor who listens,” says the physician.

Families caring for relatives with dementia, she adds, need support rather than judgement when they seek professional help. “This is because the process can often be physically and emotionally draining,” she says.
